assets.topic: Pre-incident indicators at the hotel front desk
assets.visual_frame_description: The camera holds on the marble front desk of the Marigold Hotel at 11:40 p.m. Noor, the night clerk, looks up as a man in a gray raincoat walks in alone carrying nothing; behind him the bellman stands by the luggage carts with empty hands. The guest slides his driver's license across the counter and asks for a room on the highest floor, then asks whether the room will have paper and a pen. A checklist panel on the right side of the screen tracks what Noor can observe and which predictive questions she is actually answering.
assets.player_mission: Scan the observable behavior at the check-in desk and decide which cluster of cues deserves the most scrutiny. Then identify the outcome those cues point toward, and state which questions Noor is answering instead of the ones that matter.
key_concepts: Pre-incident indicators (PINs) are detectable factors that occur before the outcome being predicted.
To consciously predict something, one must know which outcome is being predicted, or see enough pre-incident indicators to bring that outcome into consciousness.

In the book's hotel case, no luggage, a hotel near the man's home, a request for a high floor, a question about pen and paper, and giving away all the money in his pocket are the suicide-relevant pre-incident indicators.
The hotel staff were predicting whether the guest could pay and how to earn another tip, so their predictions drew on entirely different indicators than the ones relevant to suicide.
People do such things for differing reasons, and each benign explanation (lost luggage, a fumigated home, a nice view, writing a note) must be weighed before the cluster gains meaning.
A question that could give meaning to the other behavior, such as 'Does he appear depressed?', was not on the minds of the hotel staff.
Knowing the question is the first step toward knowing the answer.
Intuition is just listening, while prediction is more like trying to solve puzzles with logic, and conscious predictions are not necessarily more accurate than unconscious ones.
The man in the case handed over sixty-one dollars, all the money in his pocket, as a tip, and five minutes later jumped from the eighteenth floor.
A failure to predict is not about liability; the real point is which outcome the predictor had in mind.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests pre-incident indicators (PINs), the detectable factors that reliably occur before the outcome being predicted. De Becker's hotel case demonstrates that staff who never frame the predictive question as suicide cannot see the suicide-relevant cluster, because knowing the question is the first step toward knowing the answer.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.target_channel: Observable conduct and demeanor at a hotel check-in counter
assets.question: A man checks in alone at 11:40 p.m. carrying no luggage, requests the highest available floor of the Marigold Hotel, produces a driver's license showing an address four blocks away, empties his pocket of all his cash ($61) as a tip, and asks whether the room has paper and a pen. Which cluster of cues should most elevate concern about his near-term wellbeing?
assets.correct_cue: The cluster is the one the book identifies as the suicide-relevant pre-incident indicators: he has no luggage, he is staying in a hotel though he lives nearby, he seeks a room on a high floor, he wants pen and paper, and he gave away all the money he had. Each cue can be explained benignly on its own (lost luggage, a fumigated home, a view, a note to write), but read together they form the pattern that brings the outcome into consciousness. Noor is instead predicting solvency and tipping behavior, so those answers are the ones that cannot see what is in front of them.
distractors: His credit card bounces twice, so he must pay the room in cash from a wad of bills.
He is discourteous to the parking valet about the overnight fee, using profanity.
He is underdressed for the hotel's standard, wearing a raincoat over a t-shirt and jeans.
assets.underlying_psychology: Prediction is outcome-dependent: the same behavior stream supports different predictions, and the observer's implicit question filters which indicators are even seen. Because Noor's working questions were 'Can he pay?' and 'How can I get another tip?', the suicide-relevant PINs never entered her conscious frame; knowing the question is the first step toward knowing the answer, and the answers a person collects are shaped by the question they are actually asking.

assets.visual_frame_description: A glass-walled negotiation suite at Meridian Medical Supply. Victor, the head buyer, sits across the table from two sales representatives while a price quote is handed over. Victor says nothing, but his head retracts slightly, his nostrils flare as he takes a sharp breath, and then his chin juts forward into the space between him and the sales reps. A gesture glossary panel on the left highlights each movement in freeze-frame.
assets.player_mission: Inspect the nonverbal channel as Victor reacts to the quote and identify what his body is actually saying. Then chose the reading that matches the universal gesture language rather than the surface social display.
key_concepts: Desmond Morris's Bodytalk lists sixty-six signals valid worldwide, universal to all human beings in every culture on earth.
The majority of the sixty-six universal signals are presented unconsciously.
Everywhere in the world, the chin jutted forward is a sign of aggression.
Everywhere in the world, the head slightly retracted is a sign of fear.
The nostrils flared while taking a sharp breath are a sign of anger in every culture.
Arms held forward with the palms facing down while making small downward movements mean 'Calm down' anywhere on the planet.
Stroking the chin means 'I am thinking' in every culture.
Just as these movements are unconscious, so is our reading of them: people know all sixty-six even though most could not list fifteen.
In the predictive language of dogs, barking is a call to other dogs, while growling is the signal to respect.
Often, knowing the language of a given prediction is more important than understanding exactly what a person says.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests universal nonverbal gesture recognition: sixty-six motor signals that Desmond Morris documents as valid in every culture, most of them produced and read unconsciously. The chin jut, retracted head, and flared nostrils each carry fixed cross-cultural meanings, so a sequence of them can be read like a predictive language long before anyone speaks.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.target_channel: Universal gestures and body movements (Morris's worldwide signal set)
assets.question: Victor reacts to the six-figure price quote with a sequence of silent movements: head retracted slightly, nostrils flared with a sharp breath, then chin jutted forward toward the sellers. He still says nothing. What is his body saying?
assets.correct_cue: The sequence reads as startlement-to-anger-to-aggression: the slightly retracted head is the universal sign of fear, the flared nostrils with a sharp breath are the universal sign of anger, and the jutted chin is the universal sign of aggression. Each element is one of the sixty-six worldwide signals Morris catalogues, so Victor's nonverbal movement from fear to anger to a visible aggressive stance communicates opposition and a rising combative posture before a single word is spoken.
distractors: Victor is thoughtfully weighing the numbers and will soon concede the point.
Victor is signaling that he wants a break to consult his purchasing team.
Victor is suppressing a laugh at the audacity of the quote.
assets.underlying_psychology: The movements are produced unconsciously and are read unconsciously: the observer's intuition decodes the sixty-six universal signals without the observer being able to name them. Because the reading is automatic, the information arrives as a feeling or hunch rather than as an articulated conclusion, which is why people who cannot list fifteen gestures still respond correctly to all of them; intuition is just listening to a predictive language that precedes words.
assets.player_mission: Inspect the freeze-framed reaction and identify what the body is communicating moment by moment. Then select the reading that matches Morris's universal gesture language and explain what Victor's sequence signals to the sellers.

assets.topic: The language of grandiosity and entitlement
assets.visual_frame_description: In the reception hall of a law firm, the managing partner posts the retreat agenda on the glass wall. Mateo, a senior associate who expected to deliver the keynote, reads it and sees a younger associate's name in the keynote slot; his name is absent entirely. The camera tracks his smile freezing, his shoulders squaring, and his eyes lingering on the agenda as colleagues congratulate the younger associate. A side panel lists the seven predictive languages of the chapter.
assets.player_mission: Watch Mateo's reaction and decide which behavioral response pattern should be monitored most carefully in the coming weeks. Then identify which of the chapter's predictive languages are stacking together in this situation.
key_concepts: Attention seeking, grandiosity, entitlement, and rejection are often linked in the same person.
A person whose self-evaluation is lofty or grandiose feels humiliation more quickly than a modest, humble person.
For a grandiose person, learning he was not chosen, or was not even seriously considered, carries different meaning than it would for a humble person.
A person who cannot bear to be unheard or unlistened-to may do something extreme to draw interest if the need is great enough.
When predicting violence, we must ask what the context, stimuli, and developments mean to the person involved, not just what they mean to us.
The languages of prediction include rejection, entitlement, grandiosity, attention seeking, revenge, attachment, and identity seeking.

Believing they deserve attention (entitlement and grandiosity), knowing they need it (fear of rejection), and being committed to being seen and heard (attention seeking) combine to define the risky profile.
The conscious or unconscious decision to use violence usually boils down to how a person perceives four issues: justification, alternatives, consequences, and ability (JACA).
We must ask whether the actor will perceive violence as moving him toward some desired outcome or away from it.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the linked languages of grandiosity, entitlement, and rejection: a person with a lofty self-evaluation who is not chosen reads the slight as a major injury and feels humiliated more quickly than a modest person would. De Becker's claim is that when the need for attention is great enough, such a person may do extreme things to draw interest, so the event's meaning to the person, not to us, drives the prediction.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.target_channel: The language of grandiosity: reaction to perceived rejection or loss of status
assets.question: Mateo, a senior associate with a lofty self-image, volunteers to deliver the firm retreat keynote. The managing partner assigns the keynote to a younger associate without consulting him, and Mateo learns of it from the posted agenda. Which response pattern should be watched most carefully in the following weeks?
assets.correct_cue: The pattern to watch is the grandiosity-rejection stack: Mateo believes he deserved the slot (entitlement), his self-evaluation makes the snub look catastrophic rather than routine (grandiosity), and he cannot bear to be unheard (attention seeking, fear of rejection). For such a person the news that he was not even seriously considered carries a meaning no modest person would attach to it, and he is likely to feel humiliated more quickly than a humble colleague would; the danger is that he acts out in visible, escalating ways to draw the attention that was denied.
distractors: He is privately relieved to avoid the preparation work and quietly supports the younger associate.
He waits to be asked directly whether he wants any role in the retreat at all.
He returns to his billable hours and never mentions the keynote again.
assets.underlying_psychology: Grandiosity changes the appraisal of a neutral event: the same rejection is a routine disappointment to a modest person and a humiliating injury to a grandiose one, so prediction must be made from the actor's perspective, not ours. When entitlement ('I deserved it'), grandiosity ('I am more than this'), and rejection-aversion ('I cannot be ignored') are linked, the person's path back to significance can escalate into extreme attention-seeking acts, which is exactly the profile the chapter warns must be read as a language rather than dismissed as drama.
assets.player_mission: Observe Mateo's response to being overlooked and identify the behavioral pattern that requires monitoring. Then select which predictive-language combination best explains the situation and what it implies for prediction.

assets.topic: Auditing the guest who says he is fine
assets.visual_frame_description: A forensic interface reconstructs the 11:40 p.m. check-in of Mark Ellison, 52, at the Marigold Hotel, four blocks from his listed address. The screen splits into three panes: a timed observation log of his movements at the desk, a transcript of the exchange with clerk Noor and bellman Ray, and a baseline panel summarizing hundreds of ordinary night check-ins for comparison. The audit question hangs at the top: does the stated story match the observable story?
assets.player_mission: Review the observation log and transcript against the baseline and render a diagnosis about what the guest is actually telling the hotel. Then explain which predictive outcome the behavioral cluster supports and why the spoken words do not override it.
key_concepts: Pre-incident indicators are detectable factors that reliably occur before the outcome being predicted.
The staff's predictive questions ('Can he pay for his room?', 'Is he the authorized user of his credit card?') did not include the indicators relevant to suicide.

The book's guest checked into a hotel near his home with no luggage, requested a room on the highest floor, asked if there would be paper and a pen, and gave all the money in his pocket, sixty-one dollars, as a tip.
Five minutes after the check-in he jumped from the eighteenth floor, committing suicide.
Behaviors have multiple possible benign causes (lost luggage, a fumigated home, a view, a note to write), so each cue alone is ambiguous but the cluster is not.
To consciously predict something, one must know the outcome being predicted or see enough pre-incident indicators to bring that outcome into consciousness.
Knowing the question is the first step toward knowing the answer.
Since violence, like any behavior, has a purpose, it is valuable to know the goal of the actor when reading his conduct.
Behavior is like a chain, and the violent outcome is only one link in a process that started long before the act.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests the mismatch between stated intent and pre-incident indicators: the guest's words predict one outcome ('a quiet night') while his observable cluster predicts another. De Becker's hotel case shows that the suicide-relevant PINs (no luggage, nearby residence, high floor, pen and paper, all money given away) were visible but unasked, because the staff were predicting a different outcome entirely.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.question: Does Mark Ellison's stated presentation, 'I'm fine, just a quiet night,' match the observable story of his check-in, and if not, what outcome do the pre-incident indicators actually support?
assets.subject_baseline: Ordinary guests checking into the Marigold at night arrive with at least a bag, pay with a card, name a reason for the trip, and ask for quiet floors, wake-up calls, or checkout times. The night staff process hundreds of such check-ins; the baseline guest is solvable and his story is internally consistent.
observed_nonverbal_log: T-0:00 — Guest walks to the desk alone, carrying nothing; his hands tremble slightly as he places the license on the counter. He does not look at the elevators or the bar.
T-0:01 — He requests 'the highest floor you have,' then adds, 'something that looks out over the street.' His voice is flat and quiet.
T-0:02 — Asked how long he will stay, he answers, 'Just tonight. Maybe that's enough.' He smiles briefly when Noor hands him the key card, then stops smiling the moment she looks down.
T-0:03 — The bellman offers to carry his bag; the guest replies, 'No bag. I travel light' and walks ahead of the bellman toward the elevator rather than behind him.
T-0:04 — In the elevator, he reaches into his pocket, counts out all the cash, and presses the entire amount into the bellman's hand as a tip, saying, 'Take it. I won't be needing it.'
T-0:05 — As the door opens on the eighteenth floor, he turns back and asks, 'Is there paper and a pen in the room?'
interrogation_transcript: Noor: 'How can I help you tonight?'
Ellison: 'A room. The highest floor you have.'
Noor: 'And how long will you be with us?'
Ellison: 'Just tonight. Maybe that's enough.'
Noor: 'Anything else I can do for you?'
Ellison: 'I'm fine. Just need a quiet night's sleep. Long drive.'
Ray the bellman: 'Is there anything I can bring up for you, sir?'
Ellison: 'No bag. I travel light. Here, take this. I won't be needing it.'
Ellison: 'Is there paper and a pen in the room?'
assets.correct_diagnosis: The verbal story ('a quiet night's sleep after a long drive') is contradicted by a cluster of suicide-relevant pre-incident indicators: no luggage, a hotel within walking distance of his listed address, a request for the highest floor, a request for pen and paper, and the surrender of every dollar he carried as a tip. Each cue individually permits a benign explanation, but the collection is the pattern the book's hotel case identifies, and it is the pattern that brings the outcome into consciousness.
diagnostic_breakdown: Evidence: He has no luggage yet checks into a hotel four blocks from his home. Conclusion: the benign explanations fail under inspection, since a fumigated home or a marital argument that forces a rapid exit would still produce some belongings or some plan; the local check-in with nothing in hand is a signal the staff's prediction 'Can he pay?' cannot capture.

Evidence: He asks for the highest floor and then for pen and paper, and he gives away all the money in his pocket as a tip. Conclusion: each of these is one of the book's enumerated suicide PINs; no question the staff asked (credit card authorization, tip expectations) touches them.

Evidence: His words say 'I'm fine' while his hands tremble, his affect collapses when the clerk looks away, and he frames the stay as 'just tonight. Maybe that's enough.' Conclusion: the words belong to one predictive story and the behavior to another; when they diverge, the observable indicators carry the predictive content.

Verdict: The cluster should have brought the possibility into consciousness, and a question that could give meaning to the rest of the behavior, such as 'Does he appear depressed?', is exactly the question the staff were not asking.
distractors: He is a wealthy eccentric who loves hotels and performs generous tipping rituals.
He is sheltering from a creditor and pays cash to avoid leaving a paper trail.
He is a hospitality journalist writing an anonymous review of staff service.

assets.topic: Auditing the fight that manufactured its own justification
assets.visual_frame_description: A split-screen forensic view of a kitchen in a suburban house at 7:20 p.m. Dan is already seated at the table, positioned to face the hallway, when Priya arrives home from work; within ninety seconds the scene becomes an argument that Priya never started. A transcript pane scrolls the exchange while a baseline panel shows the couple's ordinary conflict pattern for comparison.
assets.player_mission: Audit the argument to decide whether Dan's anger is a response to something Priya did or a manufactured justification for an angry response that was already decided. Then identify the tell that separates genuine provocation from manufactured grievance.
key_concepts: Perceived justification can be as simple as sufficient provocation, or as convoluted as starting a disagreement in order to justify an angry response.
A person who is seeking to feel justification for an action may move from 'What you've done angers me' to 'What you've done is wrong.'
Popular justifications include the moral high ground of righteous indignation and the equation known as 'an eye for an eye.'
A person who feels his anger is justified by past unfairnesses will bring forth resentments unrelated to the present situation at the slightest excuse.
Pre-justified hostility is more commonly known as having a chip on his shoulder.
John Monahan notes that how a person appraises an event may have great influence on whether he ultimately responds to it in a violent manner.
Monahan's 'perceived intentionality' ('You didn't just bump into me, you meant to hit me') is perhaps the clearest example of a person looking for justification.
The degree of provocation is in the eye of the provoked.
Anger is a very seductive emotion because it is profoundly energizing and exhilarating.
The process of developing and manufacturing justification can be observed.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests the observable process of manufacturing justification, the JACA element of perceived justification (J). De Becker claims a person seeking justification escalates from a grievance ('what you've done angers me') to a moral verdict ('what you've done is wrong') and imports unrelated resentments, showing pre-justified hostility that is ready to discharge on the slightest excuse.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.question: Is Dan's anger a proportionate response to Priya's conduct tonight, or is he manufacturing justification for an angry response that was decided before she walked in the door?
assets.subject_baseline: Dan is ordinarily measured: he lets small frictions pass without comment, rarely raises his voice, and when conflicts do occur they are usually initiated by Priya, who raises them tired after work and then winds down quickly once she has been heard. He is not a man who builds arguments from nothing as a routine matter.
observed_nonverbal_log: T-0:00 — Dan is already seated at the kitchen table, facing the hallway, when Priya keys the front door; he stands as she enters and positions himself between her and the hallway, an unusually confronting stance for him.
T-0:01 — Priya mentions a coworker's retirement party; Dan interrupts with a grievance about last weekend's dinner party, saying he 'let it go' at the time.
T-0:02 — As Priya apologizes, Dan does not soften; his volume rises steadily and he plants both hands on the table, leaning forward across it.
T-0:03 — He recounts two older resentments unrelated to the topic: a check he was never thanked for and a family visit he was not invited to six months ago.
T-0:04 — When Priya asks what she can do now, Dan laughs once, sharply, and says it is 'too late for that.'
interrogation_transcript: Priya: 'I'm sorry about the dinner party, Dan. I said I'd call you back and I didn't.'
Dan: 'What you've done angers me.'
Priya: 'I know, and I apologize.'
Dan: 'No. What you did is just wrong. It's wrong, and you know it.'
Priya: 'That was three months ago, Dan. What do you want from me?'
Dan: 'You don't get to decide what counts. There's a pattern here, and I've had enough.'
Priya: 'Tell me what you want and I'll do it.'
Dan: 'Too late for that.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: Dan is manufacturing justification: the anger preceded the provocation. He was positioned and confronting before Priya spoke, he escalated a resolved grievance from 'angers me' to 'is wrong' (converting a feeling into a moral verdict), and he imported resentments unrelated to the present situation, the signature of pre-justified hostility, a chip on his shoulder. The fight exists to justify an angry response that was already decided, not to resolve anything, which is exactly the spouse pattern the book describes.
diagnostic_breakdown: Evidence: Dan assumed a confronting position before any grievance was raised, and his stated grievance is three months old and previously 'let go.' Conclusion: the response predates the provocation, so the justification is being manufactured, not discovered.

Evidence: His language moved within one exchange from 'What you've done angers me' to 'What you've done is wrong.' Conclusion: this is the book's observable signature of justification-seeking, upgrading an emotion into a moral charge.

Evidence: He brings forth the unthanked check and the missed family visit, resentments unrelated to the current topic. Conclusion: he is stacking pre-justified hostility that was awaiting an excuse, the definition of a chip on his shoulder.

Evidence: Priya apologizes and asks what she can do; Dan rejects both with 'too late for that.' Conclusion: the fight's purpose is not resolution; the apology is refused because it would dismantle the manufactured justification.

Verdict: Under JACA, element J (perceived justification) is being actively engineered, which raises the appraisal of violence as a permissible response; the observer should register the manufactured grievance, not the surface topic.
distractors: Dan is responding proportionately to Priya's repeated failures to call him back.
Dan is testing whether Priya still cares about the marriage and wants reassurance.
Dan is exhausted and misreading a passing comment about a retirement party.

assets.topic: Auditing the laid-off supervisor who only wants his job back
assets.visual_frame_description: Two camera angles animate the HR conference room of Cascade Freight at 2:00 p.m. Marcus Ward, 44, a nine-year shift supervisor, has just been told his position is eliminated. The interface presents his baseline behavior, a timed log of his movements in the room, and a transcript of the short conversation, ending with his remark to the HR director at the door. A JACA meter on the right shows the four elements filling as the audit proceeds.
assets.player_mission: Audit Marcus's stated goal against his observed behavior and decide what purpose he is actually pursuing. Then evaluate the JACA elements to determine the risk level of escalation and what the conversation reveals about alternatives.
key_concepts: Since violence, like any behavior, has a purpose, it is valuable to know the goal of the actor.
If a person wants his job back, violence is not the most effective strategy, because it precludes the very outcome he seeks.
If the desired outcome is to punish someone, there may be many alternatives to physical violence, including ridicule, smear campaigns, and lawsuits.
It is when a person perceives no alternatives that violence is most likely.
David would not have fought Goliath if he perceived alternatives; more than anything, he fought because he had no choice.
A person who feels there are no alternatives will fight even when violence is not justified, even when the consequences are perceived as unfavorable, and even when the ability to prevail is low.
Violence can be made tolerable when the consequences are seen as favorable, such as for a person who wants attention and has little to lose.
People who have successfully used violence in the past have a higher appraisal of their ability to prevail using violence again.
People with weapons or other advantages perceive, often correctly, a high ability to use violence.
We must see things from the perspective of the person whose behavior we are predicting, because each person has his own reality.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests the JACA element of perceived alternatives (A) and the principle that violence has a purpose: Marcus claims he wants his job back while choosing language and postures that preclude being rehired, revealing a different goal. De Becker's claim is that when a person perceives no alternatives that move him toward his desired outcome, or when the true desired outcome is punishment, violence becomes a viable strategy.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.question: Marcus says he only wants his job back, yet his behavior in the meeting contradicts that goal. What purpose does his behavior reveal, and how do the JACA elements shift the risk assessment?
assets.subject_baseline: At layoff meetings over nine years, Marcus is normally quiet and practical: he takes notes, asks one or two questions about severance and references, shakes hands, and leaves. Coworkers describe him as steady, and he has never raised his voice in a meeting in the three years the HR director has known him.
observed_nonverbal_log: T-0:00 — Marcus enters the HR conference room and, instead of taking the offered chair, stands near the door with his arms crossed, facing both exits in turn. This is new behavior for him.
T-0:01 — After the elimination notice is read, he asks about severance 'in full, with interest.' His tone is calm but his hands are curled into fists at his sides.
T-0:02 — Told the decision is final, he begins pacing in short arcs, twice glancing at the HR director's open laptop.
T-0:03 — Unprompted, he names the incoming supervisor three times: 'So this is Matt's doing. This is Matt's plan, isn't it? Matt doesn't know what he's walking into.'
T-0:04 — He leans into the HR director's space, keeping his voice low and steady: 'I hope you can sleep at night, knowing who's running your warehouse now.'
T-0:05 — At the door he turns back, points once, and says: 'This isn't over. You'll hear from me.'
interrogation_transcript: HR Director: 'Marcus, the position is being eliminated. There's nothing personal in this.'
Marcus: 'I just want my job back. That's all I ever wanted. My job back.'
HR Director: 'The decision is final, and I can't discuss details.'
Marcus: 'So this is Matt's doing. This is Matt's plan, isn't it? Matt doesn't know what he's walking into.'
HR Director: 'Marcus, I'd like to help you transition.'
Marcus: 'I hope you can sleep at night, knowing who's running your warehouse now.'
HR Director: 'Please take a moment before you leave.'
Marcus: 'This isn't over. You'll hear from me.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: Marcus's stated goal (getting his job back) is contradicted by his chosen conduct: relentless naming of the incoming supervisor, space-intrusion, and a closing threat all preclude being rehired, so the working goal is punishment, not restoration. Under JACA, for the goal of punishing, intimidation carries fewer perceived alternatives; his threat language and insistence that 'this isn't over' indicate he believes the fight is not resolved, and the audit should treat the interaction as a claim of continuing grievance rather than an exit.
diagnostic_breakdown: Evidence: He repeats 'I just want my job back' while simultaneously threatening the people who would have to rehire him and naming the incoming supervisor unprompted. Conclusion: violence and intimidation preclude the very outcome he claims to seek, so the words are not an accurate statement of purpose; the behavior reveals a goal of punishment, for which intimidation is a viable strategy.

Evidence: His baseline is steady and non-conflictual; today he stands blocking the door, paces, and intrudes on space while keeping his voice artificially low. Conclusion: the low, controlled voice with confrontational posture is a deliberate escalation pattern, not his normal conduct, indicating the present interaction is being performed as a warning.

Evidence: 'I hope you can sleep at night' and 'You'll hear from me' frame consequences as the target's problem, not his own. Conclusion: this is the language of a person who appraises the consequences of escalation as tolerable or favorable, which under JACA is the appraisal associated with increased likelihood of action.

Evidence: The dialogue offers no alternative he accepts; the rehire is refused, and he rejects the transition offer. Conclusion: he perceives no available alternatives that move him toward his desired outcome, and the book's claim is that it is precisely when alternatives vanish that violence becomes most likely.
Verdict: Risk elevation is indicated and the case should be managed as a grievance-in-progress with monitoring, not archived as a completed layoff.
distractors: Marcus is honestly devastated and will calm down once the severance notice sinks in.
Marcus is posturing purely to negotiate a larger severance package and will drop the tone once he gets a number.
Marcus has already accepted the layoff and is voicing a farewell grudge he will vent once, in private.

assets.topic: The eleven elements: predicting the prediction
assets.visual_frame_description: A command-center briefing room at a regional data center. Dara, the security director, stands before a wall screen showing a prediction file: a technician fired two weeks ago, a campus layout, and a timeline of reported behavior. Three managers argue in the foreground while an eleven-element scoreboard lights up and dims as evidence is weighed. The mission reads: predict the prediction.
assets.player_mission: Evaluate the team's prediction using the eleven elements and identify which element is silently failing. Then, as new indicators arrive, decide the intervention that the correctly-scored prediction demands.
key_concepts: There is a way to evaluate the likelihood of success of any prediction: measuring eleven elements, which applies to every type of prediction, not just violence.
Measurability: an outcome that is obvious when it happens, like a bomb exploding in an auditorium, is easier to predict than one without a shared definition, like 'a good time on a trip to Hawaii.'
Vantage: the person making the prediction must be in a position to observe the pre-incident indicators and context.

Imminence: an attempt on Senator Smith next week is an easier prediction than an attempt in thirty years, because fewer intervening influences apply; 'will smoking kill me?' loses significance because the outcome is remote.
Pre-incident indicators are the most valuable of the elements: detectable factors that reliably occur before the outcome.
For an assassination, useful PINs sit between too-dated factors (the assassin's birth) and too-recent ones (jumping on stage with a gun, which leaves no time to intervene).
Objectivity: people who believe only one outcome is possible have already completed their prediction, hitting the wall of their intuitive ability.
Investment: the person who must rely on you to pick him up at the airport will make a far better prediction than someone who does not care whether you oversleep.

Replicability is the cornerstone of most scientific prediction but nearly useless for high-stakes human behavior, since one cannot test whether an angry employee will shoot a supervisor by giving him a gun and watching him at work.

Knowledge can masquerade as wisdom: the executive who 'knows' that workplace-violence perpetrators are white males aged thirty-five to fifty may ignore bizarre behavior because the employee does not fit the profile.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the meta-skill of predicting the prediction by scoring eleven elements (measurability, vantage, imminence, context, PINs, experience, comparable events, objectivity, investment, replicability, knowledge). De Becker's claim is that a decision made before the full battery of predictive tests is completed hits the wall of intuitive ability, and that PINs are the most valuable element because they are the detectable part of the chain.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: Any prediction can itself be scored for likelihood of success by weighing eleven elements. The team that drops an element without noticing has already completed its prediction before the analysis is done, and no amount of later evidence can repair an abandoned element.
assets.stage_1_observation: The briefing file on Leo Han, a technician fired two weeks ago, includes his angry exit, a hallway remark that the campus 'will hear from me,' and a report that he began driving past the main gate at shift change. The facilities manager dismisses the file: 'Guys like Leo don't do things like that. That kind of thing never happens here.' The team votes to close the case and reports confidence of a quiet outcome, even though no one has interviewed the coworkers who heard the remark and the security cameras covering the gate are temporarily routed to a different monitor.
assets.stage_1_question: Which of the eleven elements has the team effectively abandoned, making their confident prediction unreliable?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Objectivity. The facilities manager has already decided that only one outcome is possible ('that kind of thing never happens here'), which means the prediction was completed before the full battery of predictive tests was run, the precise condition the book calls hitting the wall of intuitive ability. People only apply their full predictive resources when they believe either outcome is possible; the team also sullies vantage (no one observed the indicators where they could be seen) and investment, but the deciding failure is the pre-decided verdict.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Two mornings later, a former coworker reports that Leo boarded the bus toward the campus talking about 'something big coming,' and a pawn-shop record shows he bought a hunting knife. The CFO proposes waiting for 'real proof' because Leo does not fit the profile of a workplace attacker, and notes that violence 'isn't in his background.' Dara must choose the next action.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Act on the useful PINs now: station security at the campus entrances, notify facilities and security leadership, and begin scheduled check-ins while evidence is collected. The remark to a coworker and the weapon purchase are exactly the usable PIN band of the chain (between the too-dated birth and the too-recent jump onto the stage), so waiting for 'real proof' repeats the Knowledge failure where profile-based dismissal masks bizarre behavior; the prediction should be treated as live even before its score is fully confirmed.

assets.topic: When does the incident begin: the chain of violence
assets.visual_frame_description: A vertical timeline wall in a scene-review interface. On the left, a chain of ten linked links spans across the screen with only a single link glowing; on the right, an animated earthquake monitor shows the ground already in motion. In the foreground, two coworkers discuss Dale, a shipping clerk who will be dismissed Monday morning, while his supervisor Sanjay replays the week's events frame by frame.
assets.player_mission: Identify the flawed single-link explanation for Dale's possible outcome and replace it with the chain view of the process. Then decide what action the midway point of the chain demands before the Monday termination.
key_concepts: Violence is a process, a chain in which the violent outcome is only one link, not a simple cause-and-effect event.
Explaining a murder as 'He learned his wife was having an affair so he killed her' does not aid prediction.
The process of suicide starts way before the act of suicide.
We want to believe violence is a matter of cause and effect, but it is actually a chain, and the violent outcome is only one link.
Earthquakes, contrary to popular belief, have reliable pre-incident indicators; the problem is that the PINs might be ten thousand years long.
In geological terms, the next earthquake in Los Angeles has already started; the suddenness is the issue, not the movement.
An assassination attempt could be said to begin when the gun is fired, drawn, carried into the arena, loaded, purchased, or when assassination is first thought of.
Prediction moves from a science to an art when you realize that pre-incident indicators are actually part of the incident.
You would not predict suicide from a friend's job loss alone unless many other PINs of suicide were present; the job loss is a single link, not the whole chain.
The eleven elements of prediction are the same ones our ancestors relied on to survive, largely ignored by modern Westerners because life now is more about controlling risks than predicting them.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the chain concept: violence is a process in which the outcome is only the final link, and pre-incident indicators are part of the incident, not warnings that stand outside it. De Becker's earthquake analogy shows that prediction is an art when one realizes the event has already started long before it becomes a catastrophe, so intervention belongs at a midway point.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: People explain violence with cause and effect ('he lost his job, so he snapped'), but prediction requires seeing the whole chain in which violent outcomes are only one link among many PINs. Because pre-incident indicators are part of the incident, the question is never whether the event has started, but how far along the chain it already is.
assets.stage_1_observation: Dale, a shipping clerk at a regional garage door manufacturer, learns Friday that he will be dismissed Monday. Over the week he stops answering his phone, tells a coworker 'they'll regret this,' begins arriving an hour early to walk the loading dock alone, and twice fails to acknowledge the team lead who greets him. At the Friday meeting, Sanjay's manager explains it simply: 'He lost his job, and his wife left him last year, and the man finally broke. It's cause and effect.'
assets.stage_1_question: Why is the manager's 'cause and effect' explanation of Dale's condition an unreliable basis for predicting what happens Monday?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Because it treats the possible violent outcome as an isolated effect of single causes, while violence is actually a process, a chain in which the outcome is only one link. Many people lose jobs and wives without violence, so the explanation cannot separate Dale from the population; prediction requires reading the whole chain of available PINs (withdrawal, the 'they'll regret this' remark, altered routines) rather than appointing one cause as the story. Using the earthquake analogy, the manager is describing the final tremor and ignoring the process already in motion.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Monday morning arrives. A security guard reports Dale circling the block twice before parking at the employee entrance fence, and a supervisor recalls he mentioned, weeks ago, that he keeps 'a tire tool under the seat, just in case.' Sanjay must decide how to handle the termination meeting, which is scheduled for 9:00 a.m. inside the plant.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Delay the in-person termination, notify security, and have Dale interviewed or contacted offsite before he enters the building, treating the observed indicators as part of an incident already underway rather than as speculation about the future. The book's principle is that PINs are part of the incident: waiting for the 'start' (the meeting, the approach) repeats the error of waiting for the catastrophe instead of detecting the process at its midway point; the useful detection window is now, between the too-dated 'he was always steady' and the too-recent moment of confrontation.
